sources.title: Looksmaxxing may point to deeper body image issues in young men, mental health expert says
Looksmaxxing isn't just a TikTok trend, it often reflects severe body image issues in boys and young men
'Looksmaxxing' is all over TikTok. Our experts take a closer look.
A look into extreme beauty trend 'looksmaxxing' gaining popularity in young men (video, NBC News)

chunks.text: A new word has {{caught on}} online [[among]] teenage boys and young men. Looksmaxxing means improving your [[appearance]] [[as much as possible]]. The soft version is [[grooming]] and a [[daily routine]] of sleep and exercise. The hard version is [[surgery]] on the nose or the [[jawline]]. Many who follow it are still {{growing up}}, and they {{look up to}} influencers who give a face a [[rating]] [[out of ten]].

verbs.correct: To become popular with many people
verbs.wrong: To be noticed by only a few people
verbs.why: A new slang word catches on fast online, and a new trend catches on among teenagers within weeks. This word, looksmaxxing, has caught on among teenage boys and young men.

verbs.correct: To change from a child into an adult
verbs.wrong: To raise a child inside a family
verbs.why: Kids grow up fast these days, and many now grow up online, surrounded by social media. Many of the young men following looksmaxxing trends are still growing up themselves.

verbs.correct: To admire someone you want to copy
verbs.wrong: To study a problem very carefully
verbs.why: Kids look up to athletes, and teenagers often look up to older siblings or coaches. Many boys who try looksmaxxing look up to online influencers who rate a face out of ten.

chunks.text: A social worker at the University of Michigan wrote in July 2026 that these behaviors [[look like]] the [[signs]] of an [[eating disorder]] or [[body dysmorphia]]. Some young men {{cut out}} [[whole food groups]] or {{give up}} meals for days. A few hit their own face with a [[hammer]]. She says the [[trend]] is not [[harmless]], and that a boy who starts small can {{end up}} in danger.

verbs.correct: To stop eating a type of food
verbs.wrong: To spend less money than before
verbs.why: Some people cut out sugar from their diet, and others cut out carbs to lose weight fast. A social worker said some young men following looksmaxxing trends cut out whole food groups for weeks.

verbs.correct: To stop having something you want
verbs.wrong: To gain weight in a short time
verbs.why: People give up sweets for a diet, and some give up meat entirely for their health. A social worker found that some young men give up meals for days while chasing a certain look.

verbs.correct: To reach a situation you did not plan
verbs.wrong: To close an online account for good
verbs.why: A small habit can end up as a serious problem, and a light diet can end up as something dangerous. A social worker warns that a boy who starts small with looksmaxxing can end up in real danger.

chunks.text: Looksmaxxing spreads because it [[pays to]] {{show off}}. A researcher at Northeastern University says the most [[extreme]] [[stunts]] get the most clicks, so the advice keeps getting harder. He also says the [[ideal]] face in these videos copies old European [[beauty standards]]. A [[psychologist]] there says men are a new market for beauty companies. For some boys, looksmaxxing stops being a hobby and can {{take over}} the whole day. Then the wish to {{stand out}} [[turns into]] a fear of being [[judged]].

verbs.correct: To try to impress other people
verbs.wrong: To arrive at a place as planned
verbs.why: Teenagers show off a new haircut online, and some show off their workout results for likes. Looksmaxxing spreads partly because it pays for young men to show off online.

verbs.correct: To fill all of a person's time
verbs.wrong: To hire a person for a new job
verbs.why: A hobby can take over your weekends, and stress can take over your whole day. For some boys, looksmaxxing stops being a hobby and starts to take over the entire day.

verbs.correct: To be easy to notice in a crowd
verbs.wrong: To copy someone else's style exactly
verbs.why: A bright red coat makes you stand out in a crowd, and a strong resume helps you stand out at an interview. For some boys, the wish to stand out becomes a fear of being judged instead.

chunks.text: Doctors {{point out}} that the problem is easy to [[miss]] in boys. Most tests ask about a fear of being fat, so a boy who trains hard to look [[lean]] can pass them. Researchers estimate that [[one in three]] people with an eating disorder is male. The [[warning signs]] include [[obsessive]] mirror checks and secret rules about food. Experts say it is healthy to {{work out}}. But they also advise parents to help a son {{open up}} and to [[seek help]] early, since [[self-esteem]] problems can have [[long-term]] effects.

verbs.correct: To tell people about an important fact
verbs.wrong: To argue against a popular opinion
verbs.why: Doctors point out warning signs early, and teachers point out mistakes before a test. Doctors point out that eating disorders are easy to miss in boys who look physically fit.

verbs.correct: To train the body to get stronger
verbs.wrong: To follow a strict diet for weeks
verbs.why: People work out at the gym, and others work out at home with simple equipment. Experts say it is healthy to work out, but they worry when exercise becomes an obsession instead.

verbs.wrong: To admit that you did something wrong
verbs.why: Friends open up about their worries, and patients open up to a doctor they trust. Experts advise parents to help a son open up about pressure before problems grow serious.

mainIdea.s: A trend called looksmaxxing has caught on among young men who want a better appearance. Doctors warn it can hide an eating disorder that many tests fail to catch in boys.
mainIdea.why: The story says the trend is not harmless and can point to an eating disorder or body dysmorphia that tests often miss in boys.

mainIdea.s: Doctors warn that looksmaxxing can be a sign of an eating disorder in young men. But the trend usually stays mild, since boys rarely try more than a daily skincare routine.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the trend can go far past skincare. The article says the hard version means surgery, and a few boys even hit their own face with a hammer.

mainIdea.s: Health officials in several countries opened new school programs this year to catch signs of teenage eating disorders. The programs train teachers to spot warning signs fast.
mainIdea.why: This story is about looksmaxxing among young men, not about new school programs for spotting eating disorders.
